books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, D. Regional Specialization

stimulus.text:
Cotton in the American economy, from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.5 D:

| Measure | 1830 | 1860 |
|---|---|---|
| Cotton bales produced | about 700,000 | nearly 5,000,000 |
| Cotton as a share of American exports | — | 58 percent |

By 1860, American cotton also made up about three-quarters of the world's supply of cotton.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.5 D (cotton production, export share, world share). Data table, not an image.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The growth shown in the table most directly increased

options.text: enslaved labor in the South and the internal slave trade
the number of free Black farmers in the North
options.misconception: Free Black communities existed in the North, but cotton growth did not create free Black farmers there.

options.text: the movement of Southern planters into factory work
options.misconception: Planters stayed planters; cotton wealth kept them on the land, it did not send them into factories.

options.text: the use of wage labor on Southern cotton plantations
options.misconception: Cotton plantations ran on enslaved labor, not wages; the wage workers in this story were in Northern mills.

rationales.A: Cotton farming is labor intensive, so more acres of cotton meant more enslaved workers and a growing trade moving them to new cotton lands.
rationales.B: The table tracks cotton, a Southern crop grown by enslaved labor. It says nothing about free Black farming in the North.
rationales.C: Cotton made planters richer and more committed to plantation slavery, not to factory work.
rationales.D: The wage labor of the market revolution was Northern mill work. Southern cotton was grown by enslaved people.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what growing cotton needs. It is labor intensive: many hands to plant, tend, and pick it.
2. Ask who supplied that labor in the South. Enslaved workers did, and planters bought more of them as cotton spread.
3. Put it together. A sevenfold rise in cotton meant more enslaved laborers and a busier internal slave trade.
Background: Most of the cotton used in New England mills was grown by enslaved labor in the South.
Remember: a crop boom is also a labor story; ask whose hands grew the crop.
